hmls-q001.explanation: Detection and decontamination are two of the four pillars of hazmat response. Diagnosing is not one of them.

hmls-q002.explanation: The suit's activated charcoal layer soaks up chemical agent vapour before it can reach the skin.

hmls-q003.explanation: Seizures, drowsiness and collapse in many people at once point to a nerve agent such as sarin. Mustard blisters, mace irritates and LPG is a fuel gas.

hmls-q004.explanation: Work upwind so the wind carries the agent away from you, not towards you.

hmls-q005.explanation: The suit's charcoal layer can soak up only so much agent, so its protection in a contaminated environment is time-limited. The bank gives 6 hours for the SARATOGA B.

hmls-q006.explanation: Remove the casualty, decontaminate and give high-flow oxygen; your notes give cyanide poisoning an NRM. Diazepam is a seizure drug, not a cyanide treatment.

hmls-q007.explanation: Cyanide stops cells using oxygen, causing giddiness, breathlessness and cherry-red skin. Excessive secretions point to a nerve agent instead.

hmls-q008.explanation: Heat builds fast in a sealed suit, so drink plenty, skip the suit when unwell and limit your time in it, even if casualties remain.

hmls-q009.explanation: Chemical warfare agents include nerve, blister, blood and pulmonary (choking) agents. There is no cardiovascular agent class.

hmls-q010.explanation: Mustard is a blister agent: it blisters the skin and damages the airways, causing a productive cough and breathlessness. Fever is not a typical sign.

hmls-q011.explanation: Sarin is a nerve agent, as are soman and VX. Chlorine is a choking agent and cyanide is a blood agent.

hmls-q012.explanation: Atropine and pralidoxime are the nerve agent antidote, as in your notes' double auto-injector pen. Mustard care is removal, decontamination, oxygen and IV therapy.

hmls-q013.explanation: Phosgene is a choking (pulmonary) agent: it causes coughing, breathlessness and watery eyes. Blisters come from blister agents such as mustard.

hmls-q014.explanation: The FAP is in the cold zone, away from the release, so medical responders there wear the NBC suit without the face mask.

hmls-q015.explanation: The cold zone is clear of the agent, so responders wear the NBC suit without the face mask. The mask goes on in the warm and hot zones.

hmls-q016.explanation: The warm zone still carries a risk of contamination, so responders there wear the NBC suit with the face mask on, as in the hot zone.

hmls-q017.explanation: The hot zone is where the agent was released, so full protection is needed: the NBC suit with the face mask on.

hmls-q018.explanation: The bank scales antidote doses to severity: 1 for mild, 2 for moderate, 3 for severe. Moderate VX exposure takes 2 doses of atropine and pralidoxime.

hmls-q019.explanation: The bank scales antidote doses to severity: 1 for mild, 2 for moderate, 3 for severe. Mild soman exposure takes 1 dose of atropine and pralidoxime.

hmls-q020.explanation: The bank scales antidote doses to severity: 1 for mild, 2 for moderate, 3 for severe. Severe soman exposure takes 3 doses of atropine and pralidoxime.

hmls-q021.explanation: Nerve agents overstimulate glands and muscles: runny nose, vomiting, diarrhoea and growing breathlessness. Fever is not a nerve agent sign.

hmls-q022.explanation: Mild exposure brings a runny nose, salivation, nausea and vomiting. Seizures mean a severe exposure.

hmls-q023.explanation: Severe exposure brings seizures, unconsciousness and severe breathlessness. Chest pain is not part of that picture.

hmls-q024.explanation: Lewisite care is immediate decontamination, high-flow oxygen and its antidote, British Anti-Lewisite (BAL). Your notes keep diazepam for ongoing seizures.

hmls-q025.explanation: British Anti-Lewisite (BAL) is the specific antidote for lewisite, an arsenic-based blister agent. Atropine and pralidoxime are for nerve agents.

hmls-q026.explanation: Your notes: inject the atropine and pralidoxime pen into the mid vastus lateralis, the outer aspect of the thigh, and hold it for 10 s.

hmls-q027.explanation: Your notes: both auto-injector pens go into the mid vastus lateralis, the outer aspect of the thigh, held there for 10 s.

hmls-q028.explanation: Clear debris and clothing, wash with plenty of water or saline and dress the wound. Atropine and oxime are injected, as your notes' auto-injectors show, not used to flush.

hmls-q029.explanation: Casualty care means decontamination, first aid and antidotes. Setting up the hot, warm and cold zones is scene control, not casualty management.

hmls-q030.explanation: Your notes: the single auto-injector pen holds diazepam for ongoing seizures. The double pen of atropine and pralidoxime treats the nerve agent itself.

hmls-q031.explanation: An unusual smell, a gas cloud or many people with the same symptoms all suggest a chemical release. Rain clouds are just weather.

hmls-q032.explanation: Hazmat scenes are split into hot, warm and cold zones. There is no wind zone, though wind direction still matters for where you stand.

hmls-q033.explanation: Chemical agents mainly enter through the skin and by being breathed in, which is why the suit and the face mask are both needed.

hmls-q034.explanation: Nerve agents cause dim vision from tiny pupils, drooling, cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea. A rash is not a nerve agent sign.

hmls-q035.explanation: Early decontamination removes the agent, limits how much is absorbed and cuts staff exposure. It does nothing for hydration.

hmls-q036.explanation: The First Aid Point is set up in the cold zone, as far as possible from the point of release, so casualties are treated away from the agent.

hmls-q037.explanation: No one works in the warm zone without PPE: contamination is still possible there, so the suit and face mask stay on and time there is limited.

hmls-q038.explanation: Nerve agents block the enzyme that switches nerve signals off, so glands, muscles and the nervous system are overstimulated. The reproductive system isn't a target.

hmls-q039.explanation: Your notes: the double auto-injector pen of atropine (2 mg) and pralidoxime (600 mg) is the antidote for nerve agents.

hmls-q040.explanation: Vesicants are blister agents such as mustard and lewisite, one of the chemical warfare classes. Clotting, skin and binding agents are not classes.

hmls-q041.explanation: Sarin is a nerve agent, so its antidotes are atropine and pralidoxime, the double auto-injector pen in your notes.

hmls-q042.explanation: Mustard blisters the skin and irritates the airways, causing sore throat and cough. Constipation is not a sign of mustard exposure.

hmls-q043.explanation: Seizures and collapse in many people at once point to a nerve agent such as soman. Lewisite and mustard are blister agents, and mace is an irritant.

hmls-q044.explanation: One chemical release can harm many people at once, so a hazmat incident needs a large response. The bank's figure is 8 EAS ambulances.

hmls-q045.explanation: P3 casualties are the least serious, walking group, so they can travel together by the PDV. More serious casualties go by ambulance.

hmls-q046.explanation: First responders protect themselves, keep the public out and inform the control room. Going into the hot zone to find the agent only adds a casualty.

hmls-q047.explanation: Record the dose on the medical treatment card and drop the used injector in a sharps box. Your notes: document right after giving any medication.

hmls-q048.explanation: Breathlessness, cough and cramps without collapse is a moderate exposure, so P2. Severe breathlessness would make it P1; mild eye and nose signs, P3.

hmls-q049.explanation: Severe breathlessness makes this casualty critical, so P1. Milder breathlessness with cramps would be P2.

hmls-q050.explanation: With no breathing and no carotid pulse, the casualty is P0, the dead category in mass casualty triage.

hmls-q051.explanation: Blurred vision and a runny nose alone are mild signs, so the casualty is P3, the least urgent group.

hmls-q052.explanation: For a P0 (dead) casualty, mark both sides of the medical treatment card with an X so the status is clear to everyone.

hmls-q053.explanation: Your notes: press the auto-injector into the outer thigh and hold it for 10 s so the full dose goes in.

hmls-q054.explanation: The four pillars are early protection, early detection, early decontamination and early HMLS.

hmls-q055.explanation: Seizures, drowsiness and collapse in many people at once point to a nerve agent such as sarin. Lewisite and mustard are blister agents; mace irritates.

hmls-q056.explanation: Record how many auto-injectors were given, when and where, so the next team knows the dose. Your notes: document right after giving any medication.

hmls-q057.explanation: Any casualty given auto-injectors needs the number, time and site on the medical treatment card. Your notes: document right after giving any medication.

hmls-q058.explanation: The bank's PAPD air flow at speed 2 is 120 L/min at 680 Pa (6.8 mbar). Speed 1 gives 90 to 100 L/min and speed 3 gives 140 L/min.

hmls-q059.explanation: The bank's PAPD air flow at speed 3 is 140 L/min at 650 Pa (6.5 mbar). Speed 1 gives 90 to 100 L/min and speed 2 gives 120 L/min.

hmls-q060.explanation: The bank's PAPD air flow at speed 1 is 90 to 100 L/min at 710 Pa (7.1 mbar). Speed 2 gives 120 L/min and speed 3 gives 140 L/min.

hmls-q061.explanation: Responders must be decontaminated before entering the cold zone, so they don't carry the agent into the clean area.

mt-a-q001.explanation: Late rising pressure in the skull slows the pulse, makes breathing deep or erratic and pushes BP up. Your notes link a wide pulse pressure (over 60) to head injury.

mt-a-q002.explanation: Rising pressure inside the skull presses on the nerve that controls one pupil, so one dilated pupil is an early sign. Your head and face check looks for equal, reactive pupils.

mt-a-q003.explanation: Palpation is examining by touch, as when you palpate the skull, chest and abdomen in the head-to-toe exam. Palpitation is a pounding heartbeat; auscultation is listening.

mt-a-q004.explanation: With a complete obstruction no air moves, so the patient cannot cough, speak or breathe. Wheezing, whispering or a hard exhale mean some air still gets through.

mt-a-q005.explanation: In a pneumothorax air collects in the chest and the lung collapses, so breath sounds fade or vanish on that side. Your notes list decreased breath sounds on the affected side.

mt-a-q006.explanation: An infant's small face makes a tight mask seal hard to hold. Your notes stress the right mask size, a firm C-E clamp and covering nose and mouth with minimal gaps.

mt-a-q007.explanation: DCAP-BTLS: deformities, contusions, abrasions, punctures, burns, tenderness, lacerations, swelling. Your notes' DTBL neck check uses T for tenderness too.

mt-a-q008.explanation: In a tension pneumothorax trapped air builds pressure: breath sounds fade on that side, the lung gets harder to inflate, and pressure on the heart backs blood into the neck veins.

mt-a-q009.explanation: Switch the LSU on first, but apply suction only once the catheter is in place at the measured depth, never while inserting it. Keep each suction under 10 seconds.

mt-a-q010.explanation: A child's airway is soft and easily kinked, so overextending the neck can close it off and make ventilation harder, not easier.

mt-a-q011.explanation: A smoke-filled room with no burns points to carbon monoxide: haemoglobin binds CO instead of oxygen, so the brain is starved of oxygen and she loses consciousness.

mt-a-q012.explanation: The oximeter reads CO-bound haemoglobin as if it carried oxygen. Your notes: with CO poisoning, SpO2 shows a falsely normal or high reading.

mt-a-q013.explanation: Hyperbaric (high-pressure) oxygen clears CO from the blood fastest, hence transport to a hyperbaric facility. Your notes give CO poisoning an NRM, not a nasal cannula.

mt-a-q014.explanation: CO starves the tissues of oxygen, so patients turn drowsy and confused, not hyperactive. Cyanosis, cherry-red skin and chest pain can all occur.

mt-a-q015.explanation: CO comes from fuel burning without enough air, such as engine exhaust, fires and poorly vented heaters. A well-ventilated heater is the safe case.

mt-a-q016.explanation: A constricting band left on blocks the vein, so check it is off first. Your notes put 'Tourniquet removed?' first when troubleshooting slow or no flow.

mt-a-q017.explanation: Your notes check JVD with the patient half-reclined at 45°. Lying flat fills even normal neck veins, and sitting bolt upright can hide distension.

mt-a-q018.explanation: Stable angina comes on with exertion or stress, when the heart needs more oxygen than narrowed arteries can deliver. Your notes: it eases with rest or GTN.

mt-a-q019.explanation: When the left side fails, fluid backs up into the lungs (pulmonary edema). Your notes list wheezing among the signs of pulmonary edema.

mt-a-q020.explanation: Diminished breath sounds on the stabbed side, shock signs and flat neck veins point to a hemothorax, blood in the chest. Tension pneumothorax or tamponade would distend the neck veins; your notes list JVD for tamponade.

mt-a-q021.explanation: A greenstick fracture is a partial break: the bone cracks only part way through, bending like a green twig. It is most common in children, whose bones are still flexible.

mt-a-q022.explanation: The tissue keeps burning until the source is stopped, so stopping the burning process comes first. Sizing the burn and dressing it follow.

mt-a-q023.explanation: Blisters mean a partial-thickness (second-degree) burn. A first-degree burn is red without blisters; a third-degree burn goes through the full skin.

mt-a-q024.explanation: Rule of nines for an adult: a whole arm, front and back, is 9% and a whole leg is 18%, so one arm plus one leg is 27%.

mt-a-q025.explanation: Beta agonists such as salbutamol act on beta 2 receptors to relax airway muscle and reverse bronchospasm. Your notes list anaphylaxis as an indication.

mt-a-q026.explanation: Expressed consent is a conscious, competent patient asking for or agreeing to care, as in 'Help me'. Unconscious patients fall under implied consent.

mt-a-q027.explanation: An intoxicated person may not be able to make an informed refusal, so keep trying to persuade them to accept care rather than leaving.

mt-a-q028.explanation: An odd smell, many sick people and a missing first crew point to a hazmat incident. Your scene evaluation asks about hazards to the patient and to yourselves.

mt-a-q029.explanation: Even decontaminated patients can carry traces of the agent and body fluids, so take universal precautions and wear protective equipment before treating.

mt-a-q030.explanation: Young children have large, heavy heads for their size, so they tend to fall head first and injure the head and neck.

mt-a-q031.explanation: A high-speed crash with a distended, tender abdomen and a fast pulse suggests internal organ injury and bleeding. He wore no seat belt, so it isn't a belt injury.

mt-a-q032.explanation: Battle's sign is bruising behind the ear from a basilar skull fracture. Your head and face check looks for it alongside raccoon eyes.

mt-a-q033.explanation: Eyes open to pain 2, incomprehensible sounds 2, withdraws from pain 4: GCS 2 + 2 + 4 = 8.

mt-a-q034.explanation: Blood in the urine (hematuria) is the sign most specific to kidney injury; the kidneys sit at the back, under the lower ribs.

mt-a-q035.explanation: In emphysema the alveoli are stretched and destroyed. Your notes: they lose elasticity and trap air, leaving less surface for gas exchange.

mt-a-q036.explanation: An isotonic fluid such as normal saline 0.9% is close to blood plasma in make-up, so it replaces water and electrolytes. Your notes call 10% dextrose hypertonic.

mt-a-q037.explanation: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament at a joint, with pain, swelling and bruising. A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon.

mt-a-q038.explanation: JVD and pedal edema with clear lungs fit right-sided failure: blood backs up into the veins, not the lungs. Left-sided failure would bring crackles.

mt-a-q039.explanation: The position of function is a loosely curled hand, as if holding a ball. A roll of gauze in the palm keeps the hand that way on the splint.

mt-a-q040.explanation: Keep the part cool but not frozen: seal it in a plastic bag and put the bag in cold water. Ice or liquid touching the tissue directly damages it.

mt-a-q041.explanation: Exercise burns sugar, and little food means none is replaced. Your notes list insulin overdose, missed meals, excessive exercise, alcohol and vomiting as triggers.

mt-a-q042.explanation: Eyes open to voice 3, confused 4, localises pain 5: GCS 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.

mt-a-q043.explanation: Needlestick injuries are the main way healthcare workers catch HIV at work. Your notes: needles go straight into the sharps box and are never recapped.

mt-a-q044.explanation: Bruising behind the ears (Battle's sign) and around the eyes (raccoon eyes) are classic signs of a basilar skull fracture, both in your head and face check.

mt-a-q045.explanation: Rule of nines: the head is 9% and the back of the trunk is 18%, split 9% upper and 9% lower, so head plus upper back is 18%.

mt-a-q046.explanation: A full-thickness (third-degree) burn destroys the nerve endings, so the skin can look pearly white, leathery or charred and feel almost painless.

mt-a-q047.explanation: Eyes open to pain 2, incomprehensible speech 2, withdraws from pain 4: GCS 2 + 2 + 4 = 8.

mt-a-q048.explanation: Kussmaul breathing is deep, rapid breathing: the body blows off CO2 to offset the acid that builds up in diabetic ketoacidosis.

mt-a-q049.explanation: Chest pain brought on by exertion and relieved by rest and GTN is stable angina. Your notes: AMI pain is not relieved by rest or GTN.

mt-a-q050.explanation: Trauma means a possible spinal injury, so open the airway with a jaw thrust that keeps the head still. Your notes keep head tilt chin lift for no spinal injury.

mt-a-q051.explanation: Kussmaul respiration is breathing that is both faster and deeper than normal, as the body tries to blow off acid in diabetic ketoacidosis.

mt-a-q052.explanation: If a limb might be broken, treat it as a fracture and immobilise it to prevent further injury, checking pulses before and after, as your notes say.

mt-a-q053.explanation: Partly torn vessels can't retract and seal the way cleanly severed ones often do, so a tearing upper-arm wound can bleed hardest. Your notes keep the tourniquet as a last resort.
mt-a-q053.review: Traumatic amputations are usually prime tourniquet cases, so this key rests only on the idea that torn vessels bleed more than severed ones.

mt-a-q054.explanation: Salbutamol acts on beta 2 receptors to relax airway muscle and reverse bronchospasm. Raising BP and heart rate is adrenaline's job in your notes.

mt-a-q055.explanation: A high-velocity bullet opens a temporary cavity as it passes, stretching and tearing tissue well beyond its own track.

mt-a-q056.explanation: A flail segment needs neighbouring ribs each broken in two or more places. Crepitus at many points over four ribs fits; your chest check feels for crepitus and looks for paradoxical motion.

mt-a-q057.explanation: A rise in pulse or a drop in BP on sitting or standing up means the body can't make up for lost volume, so the patient is hypovolemic.

mt-a-q058.explanation: COPD has two main types, emphysema and chronic bronchitis, both mostly from smoking. Chronic bronchitis brings a daily cough with excess mucus.

mt-a-q059.explanation: Skin signs (flushing, itching, hives) with breathing trouble and low BP mean anaphylaxis, a whole-body allergic reaction. Your notes: you may give the patient's own EpiPen.

mt-a-q060.explanation: Hunger is an early warning as blood sugar starts to fall; drowsiness comes later. Your notes' list of signs adds nervousness, trembling and cold clammy skin.

mt-a-q061.explanation: Crash energy rises with the square of speed, so doubling the speed gives four times the energy. Speed at impact matters most for injury.

mt-a-q062.explanation: Exposed bowel must be kept moist and clean, so it gets an occlusive dressing that stops it drying out and limits contamination.

mt-a-q063.explanation: Pulse 68 and regular breathing are normal, and BP 128/86 is close to your notes' range. Altered mental status is never normal and may explain the fall.

mt-a-q064.explanation: One rescuer steadies the limb and checks distal pulse, movement and sensation while the other splints. Your notes check limb pulses before and after immobilising.

mt-a-q065.explanation: Each spiderweb crack marks a head hitting the glass, so two cracks with only the pinned driver means someone else may be hurt. Your scene check counts casualties.

mt-a-q066.explanation: BP 132/74 meets your chest pain protocol (SBP 90 or more) for GTN 0.4 mg. Atropine needs HR 50 or less with shock signs. EMTs also need him to be on GTN already.

mt-a-q067.explanation: Back and flank pain, low BP and weak femoral pulses suggest a leaking aortic aneurysm. Treat the blood loss and, as your notes say, transport without delay.

mt-a-q068.explanation: Your notes: hyperventilation syndrome often comes from panic or anxiety. Fast, deep breathing blows off too much CO2, causing dizziness and tingling hands.

mt-a-q069.explanation: Sudden breathlessness with coughing up blood in an older, obese patient with varicose veins points to a clot lodged in the lungs: a pulmonary embolism.

mt-a-q070.explanation: When the left ventricle fails, blood backs up into the lungs and fluid leaks into the alveoli. Your notes: left heart failure leads to pulmonary edema.

mt-a-q071.explanation: A car strikes a small child higher up, at the abdomen and chest, and the child is often thrown and lands head first, injuring the face and head.

mt-a-q072.explanation: Depression is a psychiatric illness, but mood disorder is its specific class: a lasting low mood with loss of interest. Psychosis means losing touch with reality.

mt-a-q073.explanation: The tongue can block the airway in any position, not only lying down. Blockage does depend on head, neck and jaw position, which is why head tilt chin lift opens it.
mt-a-q073.review: As printed, the statement that blockage does not depend on head, neck and jaw position is false too, so two options fit the question.

mt-a-q074.explanation: A flail segment moves in against the rest of the chest wall when the patient breathes in, so the chest moves unevenly. Your chest check looks for paradoxical motion.

mt-a-q075.explanation: A high-pitched, musical sound on breathing out is a wheeze from narrowed lower airways. Your notes: stridor is heard on breathing in, from the upper airway.

mt-a-q076.explanation: In compensated shock the body still holds BP near normal by raising the pulse and narrowing skin vessels, so skin is cool and capillary refill slow. Falling BP comes later.

mt-a-q077.explanation: Eyes open to pain 2, no verbal response 1, withdraws from pain 4: GCS 2 + 1 + 4 = 7.

mt-a-q078.explanation: A failed first breath is often just a poor head position, so reposition and try again before treating it as a foreign body. Your notes' MR SOPA starts the same way.

mt-a-q079.explanation: A heavy smoker with frequent infections, a chronic cough, cyanosis and JVD fits chronic bronchitis. Your notes: COPD can lead to right heart failure and distended neck veins.

mt-a-q080.explanation: The superior and inferior vena cava carry blood from the body into the right atrium. The tricuspid valve is the way out, into the right ventricle.

mt-a-q081.explanation: Hypoglycaemia isn't limited to diabetics: your notes list excessive alcohol among its triggers. It usually comes on fast, and hunger is an early sign, not a late one.

mt-a-q082.explanation: Bleeding inside the brain raises pressure in the skull, causing headache, drowsiness, nausea, vomiting and brief loss of consciousness.

mt-a-q083.explanation: The pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood back from the lungs to the left atrium, which then fills the left ventricle.

mt-a-q084.explanation: Wheezing on one side only means something is narrowing one airway; in a toddler that is usually an inhaled foreign body. Asthma wheezes on both sides.

mt-a-q085.explanation: Anxiety is a general feeling of unease or worry. A stressor is what causes stress, and the reaction to it is stress itself.

mt-a-q086.explanation: Rule of nines: the front of each arm is 4.5%, so both make 9%, and the chest (upper front of the trunk) is 9%: 18% in all.

mt-a-q087.explanation: A partial-thickness (second-degree) burn looks red and mottled, often with blisters, and hurts. Pearly white or charred skin means a full-thickness burn.

mt-a-q088.explanation: Low blood sugar is a common, treatable cause of altered mental status, so check a hypocount. Your notes list altered mental state as a reason to measure.

mt-a-q089.explanation: Penicillin and insect bites or stings are the classic causes of severe anaphylaxis. Foods such as nuts and shellfish can trigger it too.

mt-a-q090.explanation: Bleeding and swelling inside the closed skull push up intracranial pressure, which squeezes the brain. That is the main danger after a blow to the head.

mt-a-q091.explanation: Your notes: a normal heart rate is 60 to 100 bpm, bradycardia is under 60 and tachycardia is over 100.

mt-a-q092.explanation: Childbirth brings a lot of blood and fluid that can splash, so you need full protection: gloves, gown, mask and eye protection.

mt-b-q001.explanation: A heart attack diagnosed before is an existing medical condition, so it is past medical history; your notes' P step asks "What did the doctor say?" Recurrence compares this episode with past ones.

mt-b-q002.explanation: Your notes open the airway with a modified jaw thrust when spinal injury is suspected, as it avoids tilting the head. Head tilt chin lift is only for patients with no spinal injury.

mt-b-q003.explanation: AVPU runs Alert, Verbal, Pain, Unresponsive. Alert means eyes open, responding to your commands and able to communicate with you.

mt-b-q004.explanation: In AVPU, V is Verbal: the patient responds only to a louder verbal stimulus. A is Alert, P is Pain and U is Unresponsive.

mt-b-q005.explanation: Your notes do the rapid body survey in the primary survey, to find life or limb threatening injuries. Chief complaint, history taking and medical history make up the secondary survey.

mt-b-q006.explanation: The bank places full vital signs after the primary survey, which covers LOC, the ABCs with skin colour and condition, and the rapid body survey. Your notes take vital signs within the primary survey.
mt-b-q006.review: The notes take vital signs (with skin colour and condition) inside the primary survey, so by the notes all four items belong to it and none fits "except".

mt-b-q007.explanation: An unstable patient can change quickly, so your notes reassess every 5 minutes. A stable patient is reassessed every 15 minutes.

mt-b-q008.explanation: Your notes reassess a stable patient every 15 minutes. Every 5 minutes is for an unstable patient, who can change quickly.

mt-b-q009.explanation: The rapid body survey finds life and limb threats. The head-to-toe exam then looks for anything less obvious: your notes do it "to see if I missed out anything during RBS".

mt-b-q010.explanation: Your head-to-toe neck step inspects for distended neck veins (JVD) and palpates for tracheal deviation, so you check for both.

mt-b-q011.explanation: Paradoxical motion is a chest sign, listed under your chest step. Your abdomen step checks for tenderness, guarding, distension, masses and penetrating injuries.

mt-b-q012.explanation: Your lower-limb step checks distal pulses, capillary refill, and sensation and movement. Paradoxical motion is a chest sign of a flail segment.

mt-b-q013.explanation: Your notes give normal adult breathing as 12 to 20 breaths a minute. Under 12 or over 20 counts as inadequate breathing.

mt-b-q014.explanation: Rescue scene evaluation (WEHM) is part of your primary survey, done before you approach the patient. Chief complaint, medical history and allergies are secondary survey history.

mt-b-q015.explanation: Your notes ask whether the patient is compliant and when the last dose was taken, and say to bring the patient's medications to hospital, so all three apply.

mt-b-q016.explanation: Your notes' precipitating factor question asks what the patient was doing when the pain started. What makes it worse is an aggravating factor; a similar episode is recurrence.

mt-b-q017.explanation: Explain what you are doing, warn her before examining each part, and expose only what you need to see. Removing all her clothing is unnecessary and takes away her dignity.

mt-b-q018.explanation: Your notes ask "What makes it worse?" for aggravating factors. What the patient was doing is the precipitating factor, and a similar episode is recurrence.

mt-b-q019.explanation: The Golden Hour is the first, most critical hour after severe injury, counted from the moment of impact to effective treatment, not from when your treatment starts.

mt-b-q020.explanation: Your notes' order is head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, lower limbs, upper limbs, then back, so the lower limbs come before the upper limbs.

mt-b-q021.explanation: A tight bandage presses on the eye and drives the object deeper. Leave the object in, steady it with gauze, cover it with a cup and secure the dressing without pressure.

mt-b-q022.explanation: Leaning back runs blood down the throat, where it is swallowed or can block the airway. Your notes sit the patient up, head down, and pinch the nostrils (nasal alae).

mt-b-q023.explanation: Facial injuries can block the airway, bleed enough to cause shock, and come with cervical spine injury from the same force. The heart lies well away from the face.

mt-b-q024.explanation: Lying face down presses on the injured chest and makes breathing harder. A pillow splint steadies the flail segment, and oxygen supports the patient.

mt-b-q025.explanation: 10% dextrose raises blood sugar, and your notes give it for hypoglycaemia, so it does nothing for a pneumothorax. Oxygen, a position of comfort and rapid transport do help.

mt-b-q026.explanation: An open pneumothorax brings a sucking, bubbling wound, rapid laboured breathing and coughed-up blood (hemoptysis). Blood pressure tends to fall with shock, not rise.

mt-b-q027.explanation: Stabilise the rod with bulky dressing, assist breathing with a BVM if needed and transport at once. Bent knees are a position for abdominal injuries, not a chest wound.

mt-b-q028.explanation: Your notes' ENSAPA starts by establishing a neutral position. If moving the head meets resistance or pain, stop and immobilise it as found: forcing it risks the spinal cord.

mt-b-q029.explanation: Eyes open to pain scores 2, inappropriate words 3 and withdrawing from pain 4: 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.

mt-b-q030.explanation: Eyes open to pain scores 2, confused 4 and withdrawing from pain 4: 2 + 4 + 4 = 10.

mt-b-q031.explanation: Cyanosis and a breathing rate over 30 are signs of impending respiratory failure in your notes, and those patients get oxygen through a BVM.

mt-b-q032.explanation: With SpO2 at 92%, a little under 95%, the bank picks a simple face mask (6 to 8 L/min). Your notes, though, count a rate over 30 as impending respiratory failure, which takes a BVM.
mt-b-q032.review: The notes list a respiratory rate over 30 as a sign of impending respiratory failure, which they treat with a BVM, so the bank's simple face mask conflicts with them.

mt-b-q033.explanation: Vomitus blocks the airway and can be inhaled, so clear it first: your notes use suction for liquids. An OPA (Guedel airway) goes in only once the airway is clear.

mt-b-q034.explanation: Your notes do head-to-toe at scene only for stable cases getting Entonox. An unconscious patient still needs a blood glucose check, high-flow oxygen and an airway.

mt-b-q035.explanation: Level of consciousness reflects brain function most directly, so it is the best guide to how badly the brain is injured and whether it is getting worse.

mt-b-q036.explanation: Rising pressure in the skull pushes BP up to keep blood reaching the brain, and the pulse slows in response (Cushing's reflex). Your notes link a wide pulse pressure (over 60) to head injury.

mt-b-q037.explanation: By the rule of nines each arm is 9%, and a thigh is about half of an 18% leg, so 9%: 9 + 9 + 9 = 27%.

mt-b-q038.explanation: An object through the cheek can block the airway, and you can press on the bleeding from inside and outside the cheek, so it may be removed. Other impaled objects are stabilised in place.

mt-b-q039.explanation: Your notes list muffled heart sounds, JVD and a narrowing pulse pressure for tamponade. Tracheal deviation is a sign of tension pneumothorax.

mt-b-q040.explanation: Someone pulled from a burning basement who responds only to pain may have inhaled smoke and hot gases, which swell the airway. Airway and breathing come before shock, dressings and infection.

mt-b-q041.explanation: Your notes give a normal capillary refill time as under 2 seconds. Slower refill suggests poor circulation.

mt-b-q042.explanation: The eyes move together, so covering both stops the injured eye moving with the good one. A loose dressing avoids pressing on the ruptured globe.

mt-b-q043.explanation: Eyes open to voice scores 3, disorientated (confused) 4 and localising pain 5: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12.

mt-b-q044.explanation: Air trapped under pressure on the injured side pushes the chest contents, and the trachea, toward the uninjured side. Your neck check palpates for tracheal deviation.

mt-b-q045.explanation: Your notes start bleeding control with direct pressure. On the neck, press carefully over the wound: a tourniquet or tight bandage would choke the airway and cut blood to the brain.

mt-b-q046.explanation: A collar alone does not stop the head moving, so manual stabilisation continues until the patient is secured on a spinal board. Your notes say the buddy must not let go of the head grip.

mt-b-q047.explanation: Neck pain after a road crash means possible spinal injury: your notes keep the head grip on and apply a C-collar. Never ask the patient to turn the neck.

mt-b-q048.explanation: Your notes arrest bleeding with direct pressure and elevation, then a dressing. A tourniquet is the last resort, not the first step for a forearm cut.

mt-b-q049.explanation: Never remove or push in an impaled knife: it may be plugging the bleeding. Pad around it with a doughnut ring so it cannot move, then bandage it in place.

mt-b-q050.explanation: A collar fits properly only with the head and body in a neutral line, which is easiest with the patient supine (face up). Your notes' ENSAPA starts by establishing a neutral position.

mt-b-q051.explanation: Never push protruding bone ends back in or press on them. A doughnut ring around the bone ends lets you bandage the wound without pressing on the bone.

mt-b-q052.explanation: Opening the sterile pad right over the wound means it touches nothing else first, so the pad stays uncontaminated. That lowers infection risk but cannot guarantee no infection.

mt-b-q053.explanation: Forcing a broken forearm straight can tear vessels and nerves or push bone through the skin. Your notes check pulses before and after splinting and realign at most twice.

mt-b-q054.explanation: Bleeding is the threat to the patient, so arrest it first; then look for the fingers. Your notes start with direct pressure and keep a tourniquet as the last resort.

mt-b-q055.explanation: Wrap the fingers in moist dressing, seal them in a clean bag, then put that bag in ice and water. Direct contact with ice or water damages the tissue.

mt-b-q056.explanation: Pushing organs back risks infection and further injury. A moist dressing stops them drying out, and a plastic sheet over it keeps in moisture and warmth.

mt-b-q057.explanation: Heavy blood loss leaves less blood for the skin and muscles, so the patient turns pale and weak. Your skin check looks for cool, pale, clammy skin.

mt-b-q058.explanation: In the bank's spinal grips, the modified trapeze squeeze holds the head in line as the patient is turned onto the side. The head grip is for collar fitting; the sternum grip is for changing grips.

mt-b-q059.explanation: Your notes have the buddy hold a head grip while the C-collar goes on: it keeps the head neutral and leaves the neck free for the collar.

mt-b-q060.explanation: The bank uses the sternum grip to hold the head and neck in line while you change from one spinal grip to another, so they are never left unsupported.

mt-b-q061.explanation: Bleeding that pressure cannot stop needs a tourniquet: the bank uses the Dutch type on the forearm and the Russian on the thigh. Your notes apply a C.A.T. once bleeding soaks through the dressing.

mt-b-q062.explanation: A fractured limb is painful, tender, swollen and often deformed, and moving it hurts, so full range of motion is not expected.

mt-b-q063.explanation: Over a joint, bone and tendon shield the artery, so your notes say avoid the joint area. Place the tourniquet at least 5 cm proximal to the wound, uncovered, with the time on it.

mt-b-q064.explanation: Over a joint, bone and tendon shield the artery from a tourniquet, so your notes say avoid the joint area. Put it at least 5 cm proximal to the wound, visible, with the time written on it.

mt-b-q065.explanation: A laceration is a tear in the skin, so its edges are jagged and uneven. A clean cut with straight edges is an incision, and a scraped top layer is an abrasion.

mt-b-q066.explanation: The brachial artery feeds the forearm, so the bank presses on it next and keeps a tourniquet for later. Your notes go from direct pressure and elevation to a secondary dressing, then a tourniquet.
mt-b-q066.review: The notes' bleeding sequence (direct pressure, elevation, secondary dressing, then a C.A.T. tourniquet) has no pressure-point step, so by the notes the tourniquet comes next.

mt-b-q067.explanation: Haemorrhage is loss of blood from the vessels, internally and/or externally, and a heavy one quickly leads to shock. Blood pooled in the tissues is a bruise or haematoma.

mt-b-q068.explanation: An incision is a clean cut from a sharp edge such as a knife or glass, so its edges are straight. Jagged, uneven edges mark a laceration; a scraped top layer is an abrasion.

mt-b-q069.explanation: Arteries carry blood under high pressure straight from the heart, so arterial bleeding spurts in time with the pulse and is bright red.

mt-b-q070.explanation: The bank describes venous bleeding as oozing: veins carry dark red blood back to the heart under low pressure, so it wells up instead of spurting like an artery.
mt-b-q070.review: Venous bleeding is usually taught as a steady flow of dark red blood, with oozing kept for capillary bleeding, so "constant slow flow" fits at least as well as the key.

mt-b-q071.explanation: In the bank's spinal grips, the modified trapeze squeeze is the one for tilting the casualty to the left or right. The head grip stabilises the head; the sternum grip is for changing grips.

mt-b-q072.explanation: A head grip holds the head still in line with the body; your notes use it to stabilise the head when spinal injury is possible. Turning the casualty and changing grips use other grips.

mt-b-q073.explanation: The bank uses the spinal sternal grip to keep a sitting casualty's head and spine in line. The head grip stabilises the head and the sternum grip is for changing grips.

mt-b-q074.explanation: A bleeding forearm amputation needs a tourniquet, and the bank's type for the forearm is the Dutch tourniquet. Your notes place it at least 5 cm proximal to the injury, away from joints.

mt-b-q075.explanation: Your notes say the rapid body survey must take less than 30 seconds: it is a quick sweep for life or limb threatening injuries, not a full exam.

mt-b-q076.explanation: For heavy bleeding from a thigh amputation the bank uses the Russian tourniquet; its forearm type is the Dutch. Your notes never release a tourniquet once applied, and give 2 hours as its maximum time.

mt-b-q077.explanation: In a continuous seizure the patient cannot breathe effectively, so oxygen falls (hypoxia) and breathing may stop (apnoea), which can be fatal.

mt-b-q078.explanation: Seizures start in the brain, and head trauma, infection and bleeding in the brain can all trigger them. A pneumothorax is air in the chest that collapses a lung.

mt-b-q079.explanation: The GCS scores eye opening (the visual response), best verbal response and best motor response. Respiratory rate is a vital sign, not part of the score.

mt-b-q080.explanation: The RBS is a fast head-to-back sweep for life or limb threats, and your notes give it under 30 seconds. From approaching the patient to finishing the RBS takes 3 minutes at most.

mt-b-q081.explanation: Your notes' breathing check (NTUCP) looks for accessory muscle use and cyanosis, and restlessness shows a brain short of oxygen. A fat embolism can cause hypoxia but is not a sign of it.

mt-b-q082.explanation: In a mass casualty incident there are too few hands to hold pressure on every wound, so a tourniquet frees you for others. It never goes on the neck, and capillary or venous bleeding yields to pressure.

mt-b-q083.explanation: The brachial artery in the upper arm supplies the forearm and wrist, so pressing it against the bone slows bleeding from the wrist.

mt-b-q084.explanation: The femoral artery supplies the leg, so pressing it in the groin slows bleeding from the thigh. The popliteal point behind the knee is too far down for a thigh wound.

mt-b-q085.explanation: A haematoma is a pocket of pooled blood under the skin, often a raised swelling. A contusion (bruise) is blood seeping into the tissues, seen as discolouration.

mt-b-q086.explanation: A third-degree burn destroys every skin layer and its nerves, so it is painless, leathery or charred, and heals only with scarring. A large one can cause shock and hypotension.

mt-b-q087.explanation: Full-thickness burns over the whole body are the deepest and most extensive possible, so they are the most serious. Burns around the mouth and nose are serious too, as they threaten the airway.

mt-b-q088.explanation: A spinal cord injury can upset the nerve control of blood vessels, leaving a persistent erection (priapism), so in a male patient it can point to spinal injury.

mt-b-q089.explanation: The bank calls this whiplash: the head is flung forward into the windshield and then snaps back, wrenching the neck.
mt-b-q089.review: Textbooks usually link a head striking the windshield to axial loading (compression) or hyperflexion, and whiplash to rear-end collisions, so the key looks doubtful.

mt-b-q090.explanation: Fat from the marrow of a broken long bone, such as the femur, can enter the bloodstream and block vessels in the lungs: a fat embolism.

mt-b-q091.explanation: Bruising behind the ear (Battle's sign) and around the eyes (raccoon eyes) are the classic signs of a base of skull fracture. Your head and face check looks for both.

mt-b-q092.explanation: Chest pain, shock and a very fast or slow heart rate all call for watching the heart; your notes take a 12-lead for chest pain. A rash alone gives no cardiac reason.

mt-b-q093.explanation: Your notes list breathlessness and pallor among the signs of CCF, and a failing heart can also cause chest pain. Fever points to an infection instead.

mt-b-q094.explanation: The damaged heart cannot pump enough, so BP falls, and the body compensates with a fast pulse and breathing. Your notes list pale cold skin, rapid shallow breathing and falling BP.

mt-b-q095.explanation: A TIA is a brief loss of blood flow to part of the brain, so its signs are neurological, like numbness, giddiness and one-sided paralysis, and they soon pass. Constipation is not one.

mt-b-q096.explanation: The most common reason a seizure happens is a patient with epilepsy not taking their prescribed anti-seizure medication.

mt-b-q097.explanation: Diabetes mellitus is a lack of insulin, or the body not responding to it, so sugar cannot get into the cells and builds up in the blood.

mt-b-q098.explanation: Frequent urination, increased thirst and increased appetite together are the classic signs of high blood sugar. Your notes list low-sugar signs such as AMS, nervousness, tachycardia and cold clammy skin.

mt-b-q099.explanation: At 1.5 mmol/L the patient needs sugar fast, so the bank gives 10% dextrose IV with airway care and oxygen, and leaves out saline. Your notes' Altered Mental State protocol, though, runs IV saline.
mt-b-q099.review: The notes' Altered Mental State protocol lists insulin shock and treats it with IV normal saline, so by the notes saline is part of this patient's care.

mt-b-q100.explanation: Your notes call over 10 mmol/L hyperglycaemia, and 32.5 is far higher, so 10% dextrose would only add sugar. Saline replaces the fluid lost through heavy urination.

mt-b-q101.explanation: Your notes list insulin overdose, missed meals, too much exercise, alcohol and vomiting as causes of low sugar. Eating more carbohydrate raises blood sugar instead.

mt-b-q102.explanation: Allergic reactions show in the skin (hives, itching) and the gut (nausea, vomiting) and can tighten the airway. Chest pain points to the heart instead.

mt-b-q103.explanation: An allergic reaction is triggered by an antigen, the foreign substance the immune system reacts to; a medication is only one possible antigen. Antibodies are what the body makes in response.

mt-b-q104.explanation: The bank's priorities here are airway, breathing and circulation: salbutamol for the wheeze, high-flow oxygen and cardiac monitoring. Your notes, though, check a hypocount on any giddy patient.
mt-b-q104.review: The notes check a hypocount on all patients (A.B.E.H.) and list giddiness, which this patient has, as a reason to measure, so by the notes the glucose check is part of care, not the exception.

mt-b-q105.explanation: All three fit: your notes give salbutamol for anaphylaxis with wheezing and saline for signs of shock, and cardiac monitoring tracks the heart as the reaction pulls BP down.

mt-b-q106.explanation: Hollow organs are tubes or sacs that carry or hold contents, like the intestines, stomach and bladder. The liver and kidneys are solid organs, and so is the brain.

mt-b-q107.explanation: Solid organs such as the liver, spleen and kidneys are dense and full of blood, so they bleed heavily when injured. The stomach and oesophagus are hollow, and the lungs are air-filled.

mt-b-q108.explanation: Heat stroke is a cooling emergency: rapid cooling, high-flow oxygen and IV saline treat it, and blood sugar is not the problem. Your notes, though, check a hypocount on altered mental state.
mt-b-q108.review: The notes check a hypocount on all patients (A.B.E.H.) and on any altered mental state, which heat stroke brings, so by the notes the glucose check is part of care, not the exception.

mt-b-q109.explanation: Entonox gas expands in trapped air, a risk with the air pockets of COPD lungs and facial fractures, and it dulls consciousness, clouding a head injury. Asthma is not a contraindication.

mt-b-q110.explanation: Your notes' AEIOU-TIPS list for altered mental state includes trauma, overdose and insulin shock (hypoglycaemia). Antibiotics are not among the causes.

mt-b-q111.explanation: A small facial cut with no other injury threatens neither life nor limb, so the boy is stable. A 5 m fall, a tension pneumothorax and an evisceration are all unstable.

mt-b-q112.explanation: Your notes measure the OPA from the tip of the earlobe to the corner of the mouth, so it reaches the back of the throat without going too deep.

mt-b-q113.explanation: In dry drowning, water touching the larynx makes it clamp shut (laryngospasm), so little water reaches the lungs, but no air does either.

mt-b-q114.explanation: Your notes limit each suction to 10 seconds, as suction also takes away oxygen. They also measure the catheter, pre-oxygenate and suction in a circular motion.

mt-b-q115.explanation: Nasal cannula runs at 2 to 4 L/min for about 24 to 45% oxygen. 6 to 8 L/min is the simple face mask.

mt-b-q116.explanation: Your notes run a non-rebreather mask at 10 to 15 L/min for 90 to 100% oxygen. 6 to 8 L/min is the simple face mask, and 2 to 4 L/min the nasal cannula.

mt-b-q117.explanation: A simple face mask runs at 6 to 8 L/min. The bank gives it 25 to 70% oxygen; your notes put it at 40 to 60%.

mt-b-q118.explanation: Broken ribs hurt, the loose segment moves in as the chest rises (paradoxical breathing), and breathing becomes a struggle, so all three fit. Your chest check looks for paradoxical motion.

mt-b-q119.explanation: Your notes give 10% dextrose for hypoglycaemia, not injury. Bent knees ease the abdomen, nothing by mouth prepares for surgery, and vital signs every 5 minutes suit an unstable patient.

mt-b-q120.explanation: A bulky dressing steadies the flail segment, and slow deep breaths keep air moving despite the pain. Your notes give all trauma patients high-flow oxygen, so all three apply.

mt-b-q121.explanation: A three-sided occlusive dressing, taped after the patient breathes out, stops air being sucked in but lets it escape. Your notes give all trauma patients high-flow oxygen, so all three apply.

mt-b-q122.explanation: Air sucked through the chest wound bubbles, the collapsing lung makes breathing rapid and shallow, and falling oxygen brings cyanosis. Your chest check looks for a sucking chest wound.

mt-b-q123.explanation: A burn's severity depends on how deep it goes and how much of the body it covers, so depth and extent are judged together. The percentage burned measures extent only.

mt-b-q124.explanation: Your notes use an IV to replace fluid and as a lifeline for emergency drugs, and an IV line can also carry blood products, so all three apply.

mt-b-q125.explanation: Gagging means the patient will not tolerate the OPA and may vomit, so ease it out, outward and slightly down along its curve. Your notes allow one more try at the airway recheck.

mt-b-q126.explanation: Your notes define infiltration as fluid leaking into the tissue, from a dislodged cannula or a vein punctured through. Foreign proteins cause a pyrogenic reaction; irritating fluid causes thrombophlebitis.

mt-b-q127.explanation: Your notes put circulatory overload down to too much fluid given too fast, bringing distended neck veins, crackles and breathlessness.

mt-b-q128.explanation: Your notes: the needle shears off the catheter tip when it is pulled back and re-inserted. Never re-insert the needle; use a new one.

mt-b-q129.explanation: Your notes: a pyrogenic reaction is fever from foreign proteins (infection), with chills, backache and headache. Leaking fluid is infiltration, and too much fluid is circulatory overload.

mt-b-q130.explanation: Your notes: thrombophlebitis is a vein inflamed by a clot, from an IV left at one site too long or an irritating fluid. It shows as pain, redness and a bulging vein.

mt-b-q131.explanation: A stroke can stop a patient guarding their own airway or feeling a weak limb, so care covers all three: keep the airway open, give high-flow oxygen to the injured brain, and protect the paralysed limbs.

mt-b-q132.explanation: An air embolism is air getting into the vein. Your notes say as little as 20 cc can cause collapse, so never let the bag run dry.

mt-b-q133.explanation: Abdominal injury can cause vomiting, pain that worsens with any movement, and difficulty breathing, because moving the diaphragm over injured organs hurts.

mt-b-q134.explanation: Your notes check that the solution is the correct fluid, in date, sealed and free of leaks, sediment or discolouration, and that the admin set is in date. The brand doesn't matter.

mt-b-q135.explanation: Pericarditis, inflammation of the sac around the heart, is not an IV complication. Your notes' list includes infiltration, circulatory overload and thrombophlebitis.

mt-b-q136.explanation: Your notes' rescue scene evaluation is W.E.H.M.: witness, environment, hazards and mechanism of injury. Surveys, head-to-toe and history come later, with the patient.

mt-b-q137.explanation: BVM breaths given too hard or too fast can push air down the oesophagus into the stomach. The swollen stomach pushes up the diaphragm, making breathing harder, and can make the patient vomit.

mt-b-q138.explanation: Cooling stops the burning, but burned skin loses heat fast, so long soaking risks hypothermia, especially with large burns. The bank caps cooling with water at 10 minutes.

mt-b-q139.explanation: Your notes place the mask with its apex over the nose and hold it with the C-E clamp. The base sits on the lower lip and chin, never on the bridge of the nose.

mt-b-q140.explanation: High sugar pulls water out through the kidneys: frequent urination, dehydration and weight loss. Cool, clammy skin is on your notes' list for low sugar.

mt-b-q141.explanation: The mother delivers on her back or semi-sitting, with knees bent and legs apart, never face down. Preparing the maternity and Entonox kits and giving oxygen all help the paramedic.

mt-b-q142.explanation: Rule of nines: the whole arm is 9%, the front of the chest and abdomen 18%, and the front of one leg 9%: 36% in all.

mt-b-q143.explanation: The bank ties the broken leg to the good one with five bandages: above and below the break, across the knees, over the hips and a figure of eight at the ankles. Your notes check pulses before and after.

mt-b-q144.explanation: Tie the broken leg to the good one with the bank's five bandages: above and below the break, across the knees, over the hips and a figure of eight at the ankles. Your notes knot a swathe opposite the fracture site.

mt-b-q145.explanation: For a thigh fracture the bank ties the leg to the good one with five bandages: above and below the break, across the knees, over the hips and a figure of eight at the ankles. Your notes check pulses before and after.

mt-b-q146.explanation: A haematoma is the only closed injury here: a blunt blow breaks vessels and blood collects under unbroken skin. Abrasions, lacerations and incisions all break the skin.

mt-b-q147.explanation: His BP is still normal (136/86) while his pulse races at 130 and his skin is pale, cool and clammy: the body is holding BP up by compensating. In decompensated shock BP falls.

mt-b-q148.explanation: Your notes give 10% dextrose for hypoglycaemia, and nothing here points to low sugar. Open fractures and an unstable pelvis can bleed heavily, so saline goes in, and a fall from height needs spinal care.
mt-b-q148.review: The notes give all trauma and unconscious patients high-flow oxygen, so by the notes oxygen by nasal cannula is not part of his care either.

mt-b-q149.explanation: 2 ml salbutamol (10 mg) with 2 ml saline is the bank's dose and your notes' adult one. Your notes, though, give under-16s of 10 kg or more 5 mg (1 ml) with 3 ml saline.
mt-b-q149.review: The notes give under-16s of 10 kg or more 5 mg salbutamol in 3 ml saline, so by the notes this 14-year-old should not get the 10 mg adult dose.

mt-b-q150.explanation: Your asthma protocol runs the nebuliser mask at 6 to 8 L/min, enough flow to turn the salbutamol into a mist. 2 to 4 L/min is a nasal cannula; 10 to 15 L/min is the NRM.

mt-b-q151.explanation: Salbutamol is nebulised, so your asthma protocol gives it through a nebuliser mask. The other masks only deliver oxygen.

mt-b-q152.explanation: Salbutamol opens the airways in asthma or COPD, and your notes rule it out without that history; her squeezing chest pain is cardiac. The bank treats it with aspirin, GTN, oxygen and an IV line.

mt-b-q153.explanation: GTN widens blood vessels, so BP can drop: your notes list hypotension as a side effect and rule GTN out when SBP is under 90. Check BP before each spray.

mt-b-q154.explanation: The bank's maximum is four 0.4 mg sprays, 1.6 mg, which your notes give as the EMS dose. Your notes, though, limit an EMT to one spray (0.4 mg).
mt-b-q154.review: The notes limit an EMT to one 0.4 mg GTN spray and give 1.6 mg only as the EMS dose, so by the notes an EMT's maximum is 0.4 mg.

mt-b-q155.explanation: Your notes' aspirin contraindications include asthma, bleeding disorders and current anticoagulant use. Antidepressants are not among them.

mt-b-q156.explanation: Unconscious at 1.8 mmol/L, she can't swallow sugar, so it goes IV: your notes give 10% dextrose by bolus for hypoglycaemia with altered consciousness. Saline alone won't raise her sugar.

mt-b-q157.explanation: Your notes' causes of low sugar are insulin overdose, delayed or missed meals, too much exercise, too much alcohol and vomiting. Overeating raises blood sugar instead.

mt-b-q158.explanation: Spinal care needs a fall or injury, which your notes ask witnesses about; she was found unconscious after days of poor appetite. An OPA, watching for vomit and dextrose at maintenance rate all fit.

mt-b-q159.explanation: A dislocation brings pain, swelling, deformity and loss of movement at the joint. Crackles are a lung sound in your notes, fluid bubbling in the alveoli.

mt-b-q160.explanation: A severe deceleration crash can cause hidden internal injuries, so treat the casualty as unstable even if they look well. A simple nosebleed, a minor facial cut and 37.1 °C are stable.

mt-b-q161.explanation: Your notes call over 10 mmol/L hyperglycaemia, and hers is 28.8. Low sugar (under 4) brings cool, clammy skin; hers is warm and dry.

mt-b-q162.explanation: Eyes opening to pain scores E2, confused speech V4, and withdrawing from pain M4, so E2 V4 M4, a total of 10 on your notes' GCS tables.

mt-b-q163.explanation: Your notes' Altered Mental State protocol runs saline at maintenance rate when SBP is 90 or more, and hers is 132. Saline replaces fluid lost to high sugar; dextrose would add sugar.

mt-b-q164.explanation: The bank tops him up to 300 mg: he has had 200 mg, so 100 mg more. Your notes give the same 3 x 100 mg dose, but list aspirin as a paramedic drug that an EMT does not give.
mt-b-q164.review: The notes list aspirin under paramedic drugs and limit an EMT to GTN, salbutamol, oral glucose and the patient's own EpiPen, so by the notes an EMT gives none.

mt-b-q165.explanation: Crackles, swollen legs and a heart history point to heart failure, and your CCF protocol gives GTN 0.4 mg when SBP is 90 or more (his is 172), for a patient already on GTN.

mt-b-q166.explanation: Breathlessness with crackles, leg swelling for over a week, heart disease and high BP point to heart failure. Your notes list crackles and pedal edema under congestive cardiac failure.

mt-b-q167.explanation: Breathless with a rate of 32, he is unstable, and your notes reassess unstable patients every 5 minutes. Stable patients are checked every 15 minutes.

mt-b-q168.explanation: Your notes' vital signs are GCS, severity scale, temperature, respiratory rate, skin, SpO2, pulse, BP and capillary refill. ECG and blood glucose are investigations, not vital signs.

mt-b-q169.explanation: Spinal immobilisation with fracture management is printed twice here, and either copy is correct. Your notes treat neck pain after a fall as a possible spinal injury; his hip and open fracture need splinting.
mt-b-q169.review: The notes give all trauma patients high-flow oxygen, so spinal immobilisation with high-flow oxygen also fits this patient.

mt-b-q170.explanation: Low BP, a fast pulse and pale, cool, sweaty skin after a fall with an unstable hip and open fracture mean blood loss. Your notes' closest protocol, Arresting Haemorrhage, starts on signs of hypotension.

mt-b-q171.explanation: BP 82/58 with a fast pulse is shock from blood loss, so fluid goes in fast. Your notes' rule for SBP under 90 is a saline bolus of up to 500 ml (Altered Mental State protocol); dextrose is for low sugar.

mt-b-q172.explanation: With the airway open, your notes insert an OPA in a patient who responds only to pain or not at all, to keep it open. Oxygen, glucose and cardiac checks come after.

mt-b-q173.explanation: Nail beds show colour through thin tissue, so pallor and cyanosis show there whatever the skin tone. Your notes look for cyanosis at the lips, nail beds and ear lobes.

mt-b-q174.explanation: Vomit must come out before anything goes in: turn her on her side so it drains, then clear the rest. Your notes clear the airway before inserting an OPA; oxygen and an IV come later.

mt-b-q177.explanation: Cardiac output is the blood the heart pumps each minute: heart rate times stroke volume, the amount pushed out with each beat.

mt-b-q178.explanation: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker; your notes list it for hypertension and chronic stable angina. It doesn't clear fluid: ankle swelling is in fact one of its side effects.
mt-b-q178.review: The notes list nifedipine only for hypertension and chronic stable angina, and it is not used for arrhythmias, so arrhythmias also fits the question.

mt-b-q179.explanation: He is alert with a pulse, so oxygen comes first: your notes give chest pain patients high-flow oxygen and never withhold it. An AED is for arrest, and GTN needs his own prescription.

mt-b-q180.explanation: Cardiac compromise is a catch-all term for any heart problem, from angina to a heart attack, used before the exact cause is known.

mt-b-q181.explanation: The mitral valve, between the left atrium and ventricle, has two flaps, so it's also called the bicuspid valve. The aortic and pulmonary valves have three.

mt-b-q182.explanation: Cardiac pain is classically a heavy, crushing weight, like a ton of bricks; your notes describe dull, heavy or squeezing pressure. A toothache-like pain can be cardiac too, but is less typical.

mt-b-q183.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs, and the pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood back. Elsewhere it's the other way round.

mt-b-q184.explanation: Plaque is fatty build-up in the vessel lining, as in your notes' atherosclerosis, not part of the blood. Platelets, thrombin and fibrin work together to form a clot.

mt-b-q185.explanation: Vomiting with diarrhoea and cramping involves the stomach and the bowel together, pointing to acute gastroenteritis, here likely set off by dairy. Reflux and ulcers cause burning upper pain.

mt-b-q186.explanation: Pitting edema in both legs with good pulses and warm skin is fluid backing up from a failing heart; your notes list ankle edema in right heart failure. A clot (DVT) usually swells one leg.

mt-b-q187.explanation: Your notes: air collects in the chest and the lung collapses, with no trauma involved. Primary cases happen in people without lung disease, so it isn't only seen in COPD.

mt-b-q188.explanation: A patient who isn't breathing needs breaths pushed in with oxygen: your notes give rescue breaths by BVM when there's a pulse but no breathing. An OPA holds the airway open, and intubation secures it.

mt-b-q189.explanation: Give the oxygen and watch closely: your notes put COPD, which includes emphysema, on a nasal cannula, and say hypoxic drive builds over about 30 minutes, not at once.

mt-b-q190.explanation: In heat stroke the body's cooling fails and core temperature climbs very high, affecting the brain. Your notes call a temperature rise from outside heat hyperthermia.

mt-b-q191.explanation: Severe abdominal pain makes patients guard: they lie still, often curled with knees drawn up, to relax the abdominal muscles and protect the sore area.

mt-b-q192.explanation: Diverticula are small pouches in the colon wall, and their vessels can bleed into the lower bowel, making diverticulosis a common cause of lower GI bleeding. The others aren't typical causes of it.

mt-b-q193.explanation: Shock from likely internal bleeding needs a hospital fast, and your notes say starting an IV must not delay transport, so the saline runs in the ambulance. Oxygen and a position of comfort go with it.

mt-b-q194.explanation: Sudden one-sided lower abdominal pain, light abnormal bleeding and shock in a woman of child-bearing age suggest a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Appendicitis doesn't explain the bleeding or shock.

mt-b-q195.explanation: Triple vessel disease means all three main coronary arteries are narrowed: the right coronary artery and the left's two branches, the circumflex and the anterior descending.

mt-b-q196.explanation: Pain on exertion that eases within minutes of rest, in the same pattern as last week, is stable angina. Your notes: angina comes from exertion and generally goes away after rest.

mt-b-q197.explanation: The strip shows ST elevation in II, III and aVF, a heart attack, but her SBP is 89 and your notes rule out GTN under 90. The bank gives nasal cannula oxygen, aspirin, transport and 500 ml saline at maintenance rate.

mt-b-q198.explanation: On the strip the ST segment sits raised after each QRS in II, III and aVF, the leads facing the bottom of the heart, while I and aVL dip below. Your notes read ST elevation as infarction.

mt-b-q199.explanation: The ST elevation in II, III and aVF means an infarct, yet she has no chest pain, only tiredness and dizziness: a silent AMI. Your notes warn AMI can show up as something unexpected.

mt-b-q200.explanation: Your notes: when the left side can't pump enough blood to the body, fluid backs into the lungs as pulmonary edema. That backward failure is the patient's water in the lungs.

mt-b-q201.explanation: Your notes: right heart failure often follows left heart failure, or comes from chronic lung disease such as COPD. The left side usually fails first.

mt-b-q202.explanation: Assisted BVM breaths add positive pressure in the alveoli, pushing fluid back into the capillaries, which mask oxygen can't do. Your CCF protocol uses assisted BVM breathing when respiratory failure looms.

mt-b-q203.explanation: Oxygen comes first: her SpO2 is 92%, and your notes put a mask on below 95%. With heart disease and no lung history her wheeze is likely cardiac, so no salbutamol, and she's allergic to aspirin.

mt-b-q204.explanation: Wheezing in an older patient with heart disease, high BP, a fast irregular pulse and no lung history points to fluid in the lungs. Your notes list wheezing among the signs of pulmonary edema.

mt-b-q205.explanation: In asthma the airway muscles tighten and narrow the bronchioles, so the chest feels tight. Your notes give salbutamol for signs of this bronchoconstriction, such as wheezing.

mt-b-q206.explanation: Airway resistance is how much the airways oppose air flowing through them; bronchoconstriction narrows them and raises it. Lost lung elasticity, as in emphysema, is a different problem.

mt-b-q207.explanation: The bank's first step is oxygen by simple face mask at 6 L/min, titrated to SpO2 94%. Your notes, though, give a BVM for impending respiratory failure, which a drowsy, hypoxic asthmatic suggests.
mt-b-q207.review: The official answers to Q207 (simple face mask) and Q208 (positive-pressure ventilation, a BVM) contradict each other, and the notes point to the BVM; check both.

mt-b-q208.explanation: The bank's reason is positive-pressure ventilation, which supports a breathing effort that is failing. That is a BVM's job, and your notes use it for impending respiratory failure; a face mask gives no pressure.
mt-b-q208.review: This reason (positive-pressure ventilation, a BVM) contradicts the official Q207 first action, a simple face mask; check both.

mt-b-q209.explanation: Widespread hives suggest a severe allergic reaction, in which chemicals such as histamine widen the blood vessels and make them leak, so BP falls. The skin is usually flushed and the pulse fast.

mt-b-q210.explanation: Ventolin (salbutamol) acts on beta 2 receptors, which your notes say dilate the bronchioles and relax airway muscle, easing the wheeze. Alpha and beta 1 act on the vessels and heart.

mt-b-q211.explanation: In anaphylaxis, leaky capillaries let fluid swell the tissues of the throat and larynx, which can close the upper airway. Smooth-muscle spasm narrows the lower airways instead.

mt-b-q212.explanation: Stridor, hives, low BP and confusion mean anaphylaxis with failing breathing: support breaths with the BVM and give his own EpiPen, which your notes allow. The IV can wait so it doesn't delay transport.

mt-b-q213.explanation: Your notes: epinephrine acts on alpha and beta 1 receptors, raising BP and heart rate. Its beta 2 effect also opens the airways, so together they reverse anaphylaxis.

mt-b-q214.explanation: Your notes: mix the solution, turn on the oxygen (6 L/min first) and check for misting. Visible mist shows the nebuliser is working; never smell or taste a drug.

mt-b-q215.explanation: Unstable patients can change quickly, so your notes reassess their vital signs every 5 minutes. Stable patients are checked every 15 minutes.

mt-b-q216.explanation: Obvious respiratory distress needs the most oxygen a mask can give: your notes' non-rebreather runs at 10 to 15 L/min for 90 to 100%. A simple or nebuliser mask gives 40 to 60%.

mt-b-q217.explanation: Your notes make oxygen by nasal cannula optional when SpO2 is over 95%, so a stable patient at 98% needs no more than that. Higher-flow masks are for low readings or distress.

mt-b-q218.explanation: Your asthma protocol nebulises 2 ml salbutamol with 2 ml saline through a nebuliser mask at 6 to 8 L/min. The other masks deliver oxygen only.

mt-b-q219.explanation: Your notes list nail polish and an injured finger among things that spoil SpO2 readings, and the probe must face the right way for its light to pass through the fingertip.

mt-b-q220.explanation: Fingertips are thin and well supplied with blood, so the probe's light passes through easily, and they're quick to reach. Crews usually clip it on the index finger.

mt-b-q221.explanation: Your airborne donning order puts the N95 mask first, goggles before the gown and outer gloves last, matching mask, goggles, gown, gloves. Clean hands come before it all.

mt-b-q222.explanation: BP, pulse, breathing rate, SpO2, temperature, GCS and severity scale are all on your notes' vital signs list. ECG, blood sugar, blood type and BMI are not vital signs.

mt-b-q223.explanation: The IV cannula and its fluid are ongoing therapy, so they stay with the patient; your handover reports them under equipment and ongoing therapy. The Zoll and the main cot go back with the crew.

mt-b-q224.explanation: Never promise an exact time you can't control: a broken promise destroys trust. Staying firm, fair and courteous, reassuring the patient and empathising all help.

mt-b-q225.explanation: The bank lets EMTs start all three. Your notes let an EMT give a patient's own EpiPen for anaphylaxis, run chest pain as its own protocol, and list stroke as a cause under Altered Mental State.

mt-b-q226.explanation: Equipment must be clean and working before the next call, so it's checked at every change of duty. Your station routine checks the defibrillator, LSU and spinal boards and keeps equipment clean.

mt-b-q227.explanation: The bank's recipe is four 0.5 g Presept tablets dissolved in 1,000 ml of water, which gives 2 g per litre for disinfecting equipment.
mt-b-q227.review: Four 0.25 g tablets in 500 ml also makes 2 g per litre, the same solution as four 0.5 g tablets in 1,000 ml.

mt-b-q228.explanation: Anything stained with blood or body fluid can carry infection, so it goes in the biohazard bag. Needles go straight into a sharps box, never bent or binned.

mt-b-q229.explanation: Confidentiality covers every channel: tell no unauthorised person, post nothing on social media, and don't discuss patients where others can overhear.

mt-b-q230.explanation: Your notes list five ways to take a temperature. The tympanic (ear) thermometer is quick, clean and reads close to core temperature, so crews use it most.

mt-b-q231.explanation: Icy water cools the mouth and gives a falsely low oral reading, so wait after any cold or hot drink. Explaining, getting consent and recording the reading are all correct.

mt-b-q232.explanation: The bank puts pyrexia at 37.0 to 38.0 °C. Your notes put pyrexia (fever) at 37.5 to 38.4 °C, with 36.5 to 37.4 °C normal and over 38.5 °C hyperpyrexia.

mt-b-q233.explanation: Your notes take temperature in every set of vital signs, and each case could involve fever: a febrile fit in a toddler, infection after diarrhoea, or infection behind a diabetic's weakness.

mt-b-q234.explanation: Your notes have the crew don latex gloves and a face mask when preparing for a call, the minimum for a feverish patient. A hazmat suit is for chemical agents.

mt-b-q235.explanation: In Singapore, 995 is the emergency number and 1777 is the non-emergency ambulance line.

mt-b-q236.explanation: The bank names Lentor, Unistrong and Hope Ambulance Services as the private operators that run emergency ambulances.

mt-b-q237.explanation: Eastern Health Alliance, Jurong Health Services and Alexandra Health System were among MOH's regional healthcare clusters. Changi Frontier Alliance is not one of them.

mt-b-q238.explanation: Your notes call SCDF or police help for special incidents, such as combative, aggressive or bariatric patients. A locked door with a smell of decay needs them too; an NG tube is routine care.

mt-b-q239.explanation: In the bank's ACR layout, event surrounding records what happened and the abnormal findings, while later management goes in its own treatment section.

mt-b-q240.explanation: Going down a slope, the patient goes feet first so the head stays higher than the feet. Head-down tilting is uncomfortable and can raise pressure in the head.

mt-b-q241.explanation: Face the stretcher squarely at the curb and lift the two front wheels up first, then raise the back wheels, so the sitting patient stays steady and sees what's coming.

mt-b-q242.explanation: Log-roll him onto the PVC canvas, lift it together and lay him supine: the canvas spreads his weight and protects your backs. Your notes transfer patients to the stretcher with a canvas.

mt-b-q243.explanation: All three keep the patient safe: limbs inside the stretcher, straps fastened firmly, and a warning before you change its position. Your notes fasten all 3 restrainers with the side cot up.

mt-b-q244.explanation: Airborne diseases such as SARS, MERS and COVID-19 need full PPE: your notes' airborne set is an N95 mask, goggles, cap, gown, shoe covers and two pairs of gloves.

mt-b-q245.explanation: Raising an injured limb lets fluid drain away from it, which reduces swelling and the pain that comes with it. A splint, not elevation, keeps the bone ends aligned.

mt-b-q246.explanation: Each is a warning sign: pulling away or shrugging off the crew, a hard stare with lowered, drawn-together brows, and refusing to cooperate while smelling of alcohol.

mt-b-q247.explanation: All three are good practice: seek permission and protect modesty, arrive with urgency and introduce yourself professionally, and mind your words and manner in public.

mt-b-q248.explanation: With a patient on board, care comes first, so the ambulance shouldn't wait for a tow truck. Exchange particulars, issue the correspondence notice, and tell the other driver if it's urgent.

mt-b-q249.explanation: Other drivers need time to see you and react safely, and startling them causes accidents. Drive defensively, belt everyone in, and avoid provocative gestures.

mt-b-q250.explanation: National Healthcare Group is one of MOH's public healthcare clusters, alongside NUHS and SingHealth. The Singapore Medical Association is a doctors' body, not a cluster.

mt-b-q251.explanation: Difficulty breathing can quickly become life-threatening, and your notes treat a short-of-breath patient as unstable. A paper cut, toothache or checkup ride is not an emergency.

mt-b-q252.explanation: In Singapore, 1777 is the non-emergency ambulance line; 995 is for emergencies.

mt-b-q253.explanation: Bradycardia is treated with IV atropine, which isn't an EMT drug: your notes limit an EMT to GTN, salbutamol, oral glucose and the patient's own EpiPen.

mt-b-q254.explanation: Chatting or commenting while you examine injuries is unprofessional and can upset the patient. Explaining procedures, keeping urgency and avoiding provocation are your duties.

mt-b-q255.explanation: Your notes call for SCDF or police assistance with combative or aggressive patients, and a drunk man with a broken bottle who won't cooperate is a danger to the crew.

mt-b-q256.explanation: You can only assess the patient once you reach the scene: get dispatched, travel there, position the vehicle safely, report to the control room, then assess.
